criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale - Include the following required information: • What is the spacecraft's primary mission? • Why is the mission needed? • How many spacecraft are used and why? • Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: The report explains the reef-monitoring mission and its Australian environmental rationale, justifies a single spacecraft, and identifies likely government/science users. Operator and customers are not clearly distinguished, and the rationale and user discussion have limited supporting references, so this is at the lower end of Accomplished.

evidence.quote: The ZYZZsat however, does not require such constant coverage as the reef bleaching events occur over days and weeks. Thus, only one satellite is required.
The proposed satellite would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM) for research and/or education.

criteria.name: Main body: mission design - Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate - Include relevant screenshots and software files (in the main body of the report and/or appendix) - Include the following information: • Where it will launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? • What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? • Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? • Which ground control facilities will you use? • How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? • How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: The report addresses launch, orbit and elements, manoeuvres, ground access, duration and EOL, and includes STK-derived material. However, the proposed Vega E is not a credible 2025 launch choice; launch compatibility and selection are not demonstrated. Orbit choices and access results have limited validation, ground-station suitability is not established, and the EOL plan is incomplete and internally inconsistent. No software files are evident.

evidence.quote: The proposed satellite will thus use the Vega E rocket as a launch vehicle – launched from the Guiana Space Centre Spaceport.
Specifically, an altitude of 600km requires a mean inclination of $ 97.7924^{\circ} $ for the satellite to remain sun-synchronous.
An average contact duration of almost ten minutes was achieved, in addition to the already frequent amount of passes.
A span of five years is a sound estimate of the useful lifespan of the proposed satellite.

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.reasoning: The conclusion recaps the principal design choices and notes launch uncertainty, but mostly restates the proposal. It does not draw detailed conclusions from quantified performance evidence or resolve the significant feasibility and EOL uncertainties.

evidence.quote: A polar sun-synchronous orbit allows for consistent illumination of the oceans while maintaining a constant sun angle.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: The report has a recognizable engineering structure, executive summary, bibliography, and useful plots and data. Presentation is weakened by inconsistent figure labelling/captions, malformed or incomplete references, use of Wikipedia as a source, and grammar/wording errors. Figures are not consistently identified by number and title.

evidence.quote: This report outlines the intended designs and procedures involved in the construction of a Earth observation satellite
The following ground track details both ascending and descending orbital paths, illustrating the abundance of ground station contact time

technical_issues.issue: Vega E is presented as a likely 2025 launch vehicle, but Vega E was not an operational launcher and did not make its first launch in 2024; this undermines the proposed launch plan. The stated future launch schedule and rideshare availability are not substantiated.

The claim that two launch windows per day follow because the launch-site latitude is lower than the target inclination is oversimplified. Actual launch azimuth, range-safety constraints, target RAAN and rideshare orbit determine feasible windows.

At 600 km altitude, a near-circular orbit has a period of about 97 minutes, but the report does not give a period or demonstrate that the selected RAAN and launch date can deliver the stated elements. RAAN is not determined simply by the launch facility location.

The report says the orbit has a constant sun angle and provides uniform illumination, but does not specify local solar time of the ascending/descending node. SSO fixes local solar time at a given latitude; it does not guarantee constant illumination conditions for every imaging pass.

A single 600 km spacecraft cannot image the entire 250 km-wide reef at adequate resolution merely by selecting this altitude. Sensor swath, optical resolution, pointing, cloud cover and revisit/coverage requirements are not specified or analysed.

Mount Pleasant Radio Observatory is identified as a radio astronomy facility, but the report does not establish that it has suitable spacecraft TT&C antennas, frequency authorizations, or operational control capability. Pass access alone does not demonstrate a usable communications link.

The access table includes a duplicated access entry and a first listed interval with no access number; the claim of frequent contact is not reconciled with the reported gaps between passes or the time window represented.

The report first says an EOL orbital manoeuvre occurs, then states the spacecraft has no thrusters and relies on a passive drag sail. A deployable drag sail is a plausible concept but requires design, reliability and lifetime/deorbit analysis; none is provided.

The report describes a circular orbit as having undefined argument of perigee and true anomaly, but does not give a fully specified nonsingular alternative set including a reference epoch and phase; the stated argument of latitude alone is insufficient for reproducibility.

overall: The submission presents a coherent Australian reef-monitoring concept with substantial mission-section coverage and STK outputs. Its strongest limitations are an infeasible launch assumption, insufficiently substantiated orbit and communications design, and an incomplete EOL plan. The report’s figures and referencing also need more professional treatment.

feedback.summary: You present a coherent Australian reef-monitoring concept, explain why one spacecraft may meet the mission need, and include STK-derived design material. To strengthen the report, resolve the launch and end-of-life inconsistencies, validate the orbit and communications claims with supporting analysis, and make the conclusions and presentation more rigorous.
next_steps: Replace the Vega E proposal with a launch option supported by evidence of operational status, schedule, rideshare availability and compatibility with your target orbit; justify feasible launch windows using the actual constraints.

Validate the orbit and ground segment: provide a reproducible orbital state with epoch and phase, analyse sensor coverage and revisit needs, and demonstrate that the ground station has suitable TT&C capability and that access data support your contact claims.
Reconcile the EOL approach and support it with a drag-sail deployment and deorbit/lifetime analysis; then draw conclusions from quantified results and improve figure captions, references and editing.

criteria.C1: Your Introduction explains the reef-monitoring purpose, Australian rationale, single-spacecraft choice and likely government and science users. To strengthen this further, distinguish the spacecraft operator from customers and support the mission need and user roles with relevant references, moving beyond the lower end of Accomplished.
criteria.C2: Your Launch, Orbit, Ground Control & Communications, and Mission Duration & EOL sections address the required design topics and include STK material. For Accomplished, replace the unsupported Vega E plan, validate orbital elements and coverage, demonstrate ground-station TT&C suitability and reconcile the conflicting EOL manoeuvre/drag-sail claims with evidence and calculations.
criteria.C3: Your Conclusion recaps the principal design choices and acknowledges launch uncertainty. To reach Accomplished, use quantified evidence from the report to assess whether the design meets the reef-monitoring needs, and explicitly resolve or qualify key feasibility and EOL uncertainties rather than mainly restating the proposal.
criteria.C4: Your report has a recognizable engineering structure, an Executive Summary, a bibliography and useful plots and data. To reach Accomplished, use consistent figure numbers and informative captions, ensure references are complete and properly cited, rely on appropriate technical sources, and edit grammar and wording for a professional report style.
